Well there are multiple things going on here. You can make relatively arbitrary racial categories based on concurring phenotypes and compare these groups. Sometimes this makes a lot of sense. For example certain antipsychotics give a lot of side effects to those with African Ancestry as compared to those with European Ancestry. So here there is a clear biological distinction between groups that influences the effect of medication.

But at other times it makes less sense. For example one could compare the average income of those that identify as African American vs those that identify as European Americans. Although this research will give some insight, one can not conclude that 'race' influences income. This research is more difficult to interpret and laymen/media will probably conclude that races influences income. And this might lead to political actions.

Finally, in genetic research, one has to correct for population stratification. If you do not correct for population stratification, then you can find the 'chopstick' gene. That means that if you do genetic research to test whether SNPs are associated with the use of chopsticks, you have to correct for the fact that your sample will include asians. If you do not correct, you find a gene that is associated with the use of chopsticks, but this gene actually just shows that there are two populations.

So concluding, yes be careful when using 'race' in research, especially because race are arbitrary human made categories.
